THE STUFF THAT DREAMS ARE MADE OF

Down through the cinematic ages, science fiction films have often attempted to portray mankind's first encounter with beings from outer space, and the results have been varied. The aliens we met during the 1950s, for instance, tended to be anything but friends, threatening to invade our bodies, crush our spirits and involve us in a cold war of the worlds. Of course, there were a few exceptions like the concerned Klaatu but, all in all, these creatures seemed to be a terribly unfriendly lot. Fortunately, by the mid and late Sixties mankind started encountering a far more classy group - aliens who were supreme beings or even the guardians of our race, from the dawn of time to 2001 and beyond. And, in 1977, a close encounter of the third kind introduced particularly sympathetic otherworlders who were soon followed by the equally congenial E.T. But now with Explorers, mankind's first encounter takes a surprisingly different turn. In Paramount Picture's summer excursion, three young teenage boys experience strange dreams that teach them how to build a spaceship. After numerous mishaps, they launch themselves on an adventure into the stars that eventually brings them face to face with the source of those strange dreams - creatures perhaps best described as 'couch potatoes' from outer space - intergalactic media junkies whose impressions of earth have been formed by intercepting video signals of TV shows and old movies. This humorous and offbeat vision of one kind of alien intelligence is the work of director Joe Dante, who previously helmed the equally unconventional Gremlins, The Howling, Piranha and the third segment of Twilight Zone - The Movie. He accepted the Explorers assignment right on the heels of two years' work on Gremlins, a film that was not only his most successful to date, but also his most exhausting. "I really thought I was too tired to do this picture and, you know, as it turned out I was right," Dante quipped, only half in jest. "But I liked Eric Luke's script and I thought after the stuff I had been doing, there was a little bit more emphasis on the characters and a little bit less on pyrotechnics. It captured the feeling that kids have when they build spaceships or forts, and the feeling that they actually do it because, 'Why not?' One of the reasons kids actually do things like that is because nobody has told them yet that it won't work. It was just the kind of thing that when I was a kid, I wanted to believe could be true. With Explorers, I also fooled myself into believing that this was a nice little picture because it had kids in it and because not really a lot happens in the picture. Then you start adding that in and suddenly it begins to get complicated." While such complications inevitably came up, the most significant obstacle facing the production was evident from the start. Paramount, eager to have Explorers as their major summer release for 1985, had been trying to get the movie made for some time before Dante became involved. Director Wolfgang Petersen, in fact, was briefly connected with the picture; but the studio eventually rejected his notion of making it at studios in Germany. Despite this delay, however, Paramount remained determined to have the film ready for their desired summer release date and, as a result, when Dante signed onto the project in July 1984, he was given exactly one year to complete it - a time frame that had caused havoc for the makers of last year's Ghostbusters and this summer's The Goonies and Back to the "It got to the point that this picture would either get made with me or without me - they weren't going to wait," Dante explained. "And although I felt the time schedule was not to my liking, I just wanted to do it, so I did." Signing on board with him were executive producer Michael Finnell, his longtime friend and colleague, along with producers Edward S. Feldman and David Bombyk - the team that produced Witness- who had first discovered Luke's script and taken it to Paramount. Given the severe deadline, the making of Explorers proved to be a mad race against the clock to complete the $23 million production. To help in reaching the finish line on time, the filmmakers enlisted the aid of three different effects operations. First, Omnibus Computer Graphics was asked to design and animate two elaborate dream sequences set in a computer landscape. Second, the effects team at Lucasfilm's Industrial Light and Magic was contracted to create close to 140 different visual effects, including an invisible spherical forcefield, spaceships and a magical flight sequence. And, to complete the triad, special makeup effects designer Rob Bottin was hired to design and build the alien beings responsible for the entire adventure. All three worked separately, yet in conjunction, so that - under Dante's direction - their various efforts would ultimately combine together to create a cohesive film. "Explorers was amazing in all the things we were trying to accomplish in a short period," explained Ralph Winter, visual effects coordinator between Omnibus, ILM and the production staff. "Not only did we have very complicated visual effects being done at ILM, but there were also computerized dreams being done by Omnibus and mechanical effects that were called for on almost every page of the script. And on the set we had video playback where we had to play back clips from films. We article by also had exotic makeup, aerial plate photography, location Adam Eisenberg work, studio work, night work - you name it and we did it."

Boyle alien ship set. 6 4 CINEFEX 23 Explorers begins with a vision of a vast computer landscape - a flat, colorful schematic that extends off into the horizon. As we gracefully fly over it, we realize that it is all part of a dream - the first of three in the film. This one, dreamt by a boy named Ben Crandall (Ethan Hawke), reveals the schematic necessary to build a powerful forcefield. In the second dream, which occurs later in the story, all three boys individually imagine themselves flying amid a more complex three-dimensional computer circuit board that reveals to them more about the mysterious field and how they can use it to successfully fly into space. In the context of the film, these dreams are the creations of aliens in deep space who use them as a way to contact the kids. In reality, however, they are carefully designed computer images created by Omnibus Computer Graphics, a company which had previously contributed animation effects for Star Trek III: The Search for Spock. "We initially went with computer graphics because we wanted the sequences to look a little bit different," Dante explained, "but we didn't want them to look like The Last Starfighter or Tron. Not that those pictures looked bad. They got such flak because that look was expected to carry the entire picture; but what happens is that after a while, the novelty of the effect begins to wear off as you get used to seeing it. In Explorers, the computer graphics are used sparingly enough to stay interesting. It's not a lot of people trapped in a computer for a whole movie." While Dante had strong notions about how the computer effects should be incorporated into the film, he essentially removed himself from the practical side of how Omnibus would achieve them. "I'm ashamed to tell you that there are certain aspects of the production I was not able to keep close tabs on; and one that I immediately assumed might be able to best survive my absence was the computer material, because I'm not as knowledgeable or as computer-wise as other people might be. And since Ralph Winter and Eric Luke and Mike Finnell all seemed to have a handle on that, I let them do a lot of the planning and I just looked in at various stages of completion." Entering the Hollywood division of Omnibus, located on the Paramount studio lot, is like stepping onto a movie set from Wargames or Colossus - The Forbin Project. There, a second floor office lined with glass windows overlooks a large, blackwalled computer room down below. A bright red, metal stairwell connects the two lower rooms, and the computer room itself is filled with a type of technology that fifteen years ago was science fiction. In this facility, creative supervisor Art Durinski oversaw the work for Explorers using the Omnibus F-1, a computer system purchased from Information International Inc. (Triple-I), the company which had produced landmark computer effects for such films as Tron and Looker. Durinski, a veteran of both films, had suggested that Omnibus purchase the system when Triple-l closed down its computer simulation division several years ago. F-1 refers to the whole generic system that includes the mainframe computer and the software used to produce high-resolution graphics.

The dream sequences first began as detailed storyboards, drawn by Durinski, Steve Yiu and Michiko Suzuki to include not only the basic designs of the computer landscapes, but also their colors and general ambience. Once approved, these boards were then redrawn with more detail and ultimately digitized into the computer. In preparing these sketches, actual computer schematics and computer chipboard diagrams were used for reference. In addition, Durinski tried to consider the look of real urban landscapes to give the computer world a look similar to our own. "What we wanted to do was have a contrast so that the camera would fly over a section that was heavily populated with objects, and then fly over another section that was rather empty. We wanted to create the contrasts that you see in real cities where there are areas of intense concentration, maybe housing tracts, and then others that are more rural like farmland." This basic approach was used for both the first and second dreams. However, while the first dream was based on a flat computer schematic, the second offered opportunities to show a much more urban-looking cityscape because it was based on a three-dimensional computer chipboard. Set at dusk, this dream actually begins with aerial footage looking down on the Northern California town of Petaluma where exteriors for the film were shot. This footage, taken by Winter and a second unit crew, reveals the real cityscape of trees, homes and streets. As the sequence progresses, the real cityscape dissolves away into a completely computer-generated three-dimensional city. Lamentably, time constraints prevented a full realization of the live-action to computer image dissolve, resulting in the scene's being pulled from the film shortly before release.) In designing the sequence, Durinski not only used the same concept he had for the first dream, but went one step further to mimic real elements from the town of Petaluma itself. For instance, objects such as grain silos were reflected on the computer board by tall cylindrical objects. Then, in addition to these more realistic elements, other objects were added that are totally foreign to both cities or circuit boards. "We incorporated objects that would build up the surrealness of the landscape," Durinski explained. "For instance, things that looked more low-tech than the high-tech of a computer board - like bent pipes, elbow-shaped pipes, gaskets and rotating gears. There's even a carburetor valve which rotates like that on a car. These all echoed a similar theme to what production designer Bob Boyle used in his designs for the interior of the alien spaceship towards the end of the film. We took advantage of this low-tech idea, which gives it more of an industrial-age look. We also threw in lots of other elements, and I think it really worked. It took the computer graphics beyond the traditional circuit board. "In both dreams, we were trying to go for a look of ambiguity. For instance, in the second dream, Joe suggested that when we make the transition from the actual plate in Petaluma into the computer plate, the audience should not at first be sure of what it is seeing, It could be either a real image or a computergenerated image of a computer chipboard. In both dreams, we were going for that notion of: 'What am I seeing? Is it real, is it not real?' - especially at the beginning of the sequences. Then, once you get over into the area where it is definitely a schematic or a circuit board, we wanted it to look like a surreal environment - not as outlandish as something Salvador Dali would do, but surreal, with the flight and motion being very dreamlike Once the basic black-and-white drawings were digitized into the computer, they were further refined by Georgia Sproull and Michael Kory. Then the motion of the camera was mapped out by Harold Buchman, John Howard and Bill Dungan. The next step was to add color. In choosing colors for the two dreams, Durinski opted for uncharactertically subdued tones. "One of the disadvantages of computer graphics at times is that it's very easy to use stylized, saturated colors, and then all of a sudden the computer graphic stands out. However, within the context of what we were doing for Explorers, we wanted to be subdued; we wanted it to basically fit the mood and the feeling, visually, of celingke sully everything else in the film. We also had to make sure the imagery worked within the context of other live-action elements and that it blended in with the work that ILM was doing." Omnibus' carefully produced efforts provided Explorers with approximately two minutes of computer-generated dream footage - footage that was composited by ILM and married with additional effects from the Marin County facility - including foreground clouds. In addition to the two dreams, Omnibus also provided the monitor graphics that are seen on the boys' home computer. For these, a VAX 11/780 system was initially used to create the readouts which were then transferred to a computer system called Iris. Iris is a real-time, motion preview playback system that allowed operator Doug MacMillan to play back sequences or even create new ones right on the set. The first dream reveals to Ben and his friends how to construct the schematic necessary to create a powerful forcefield. While this spherical field eventually grows large enough to contain the boys' ship, its first appearance in the film is as a tiny bubble floating in the basement laboratory of Ben's friend, Wolfgang Muller (River Phoenix). Wolf is a computer whiz who turns the schematic that Ben copied down after his dream into a workable computer-controlled reality. However, while Wolf knows howto build the forcefield, he does not immediately understand how to control it and, within a matter of a few seconds after its activation, the field nearly demolishes his basement. Creating this bubble-like forcefield was just one of the many challenges that faced the staff at ILM, and while it may not have been the most difficult to execute, it was one of the most crucial. From the earliest storyboards drawn by effects art director Nilo Rodis and Phill Norwood, visual effects supervisor Bruce Nicholson knew the forcefield itself would be one of the most important effects in the film. Ultimately, we found the UV to be the most interesting. It gave the ball a certain degree of transparency and a certain amount of luminescence which helped the bubble look more round. It also made it more three-dimensional-looking, and that was what we wanted. We then took some stills of the ball under the UV light and had transparencies made from them. The transparencies had a real neat UV glow on them that we used to represent the glow of the edge of the forcefield." In practice, the transparencies were placed on the animation stand and rephotographed by a camera that replicated the moves done on background plates which had been shot on the set of Wolfgang's basement laboratory. Then, in addition to the outline provided by the transparencies, the bubble was enhanced by two other animation techniques. First, animated highlights were incorporated into the shots to create reflections of the basement room lights on the bubble. Second, and perhaps most importantly, the background of the room seen through the ball had to be distorted to imitate the look of real bubbles. This distortion was particularly necessary for shots where the outline of the bubble itself would not be completely visible. As a means of visualizing the invisible, animation supervisor Bruce Walters suggested that the forcefield could easily be detected by the distortion it created. When someone looked at the sphere, they would see the background behind it distorted by the field. "In other words," Nicholson elaborated, "animation would shoot us a bubble, which would be the rephotographed element made from the transparency of the ball under UV light. They would also shoot a holdout matte which would be a silhouette of the shape of the bubble. Then, using that matte, we would hold out the background seen through the bubble and replace it with a distortion of that background. This distortion would simply be a size change of the background itself. So this resulted in essentially two background plates - one that was normal size and one that was not. Then we put the distorted size within the area of the bubble. "The actual distortion was anywhere from around five percent to roughly twenty percent. It would vary in size depending on the background. Generally, we made it smaller because that seemed to work better. The distortion was all done in the optical step - in the intermediate step of the composite. Since we were shooting all of our plates in VistaVision, we had to get back to 4-perf standard size when our work was completed. So, in the intermediate step, we would produce all of these elements - the distortion background element, the bubble glow, the bubble highlight and a crescent enhancement. Then we put that all together in the final composite which would be in 1.66 aspect ratio, and it worked out fine. We weren't going any extra generations in our composite process in order to accomplish that, so the quality of the image was very good." Of the numerous bubble shots in the film, the most important was the establishing shot because it had to completely convince the audience that such a forcefield was possible. As a result, that

shot had to have the most detail and was ultimately the most complex. "We actually developed some artwork to make you believe it was a sphere instead of a disk," Rodis said. "The particular case was when the kids were looking straight into the camera lens, and between the lens and the kids was supposed to be the bubble. Well, neither one of the boys was looking at the same spot and we had to convince the audience and ourselves that the bubble was actually floating between them. What that really meant was drawing the bubble out from the two-dimensional surface of the film, and the only way we could think of doing that was to bring in highlights and make those highlights move, even though they really shouldn't have. So, we had to cheat some by suggesting that the source of the light in the basement was moving when the ball was essentially remaining in the same place. "After that shot, the bubble starts moving around the basement, and it becomes a kinetic joke - you are no longer watching it, you are watching what it is doing. So, at that point, we felt we could drop all the complexity that we had come up with to convince the audience of what it was. It was very important for us to isolate that shot; and once we had, everything else fell into place. In all of the shots that we did of the bubble, we also added a blur, which was sort of a soft distortion; and if we felt something was missing, we added further highlights. Every shot was tailored to make sure that the audience didn't feel that something was missing." When the forcefield does begin zipping around the room, it sweeps through like a wild tornado. The incident occurs when one of Wolf's cats decides to stroll across the computer keyboard, sending the forcefield into a frenzy. It flies across the room, burns a hole through the side of a piano, races under the keys and then pops out the other side. Then it rounds a corner, knocks down a few of the boards holding up the ceiling, burns through a steam pipe causing steam to shoot out of the pipe, burns a hole through a vertical support post, crashes through several bottles and knocks the head off a toy monkey. The actual destruction caused by the bubble was supervised by physical effects coordinator Robert MacDonald and his assistant Dennis Peterson. For most of the effects, air rams and minor explosives were used to manifest the impact of the free-flying energy fielu. On the piano, for instance, precut holes on either side of the reyboard were rigged with a piece of primacord explosive. Then, to make the keys drop down as the sphere raced underneath them, the keys were rigged with a piece of iron that was on a cable. The iron, attached to an air ram. went across the keys from behind the front board of the piano. When the cable holding it was pulled, a microswitch caused the primacord to knock out an oval on one side of the keyboard. Then the iron pulled across under the keys causing them to drop down. When it reached the end of the keyboard, it hit yet another microswitch causing the second oval to fall out. Similar effects were used on the bookshelf -causing all the books to compact together - the vertical post and a chair with a pillow on it that, when 12 * CINEFEX 23

pierced by the field, sends feathers shooting across the room. All of this action was filmed on VistaVision plates by ILM, enabling Nicholson, along with cameramen Mike Owens and Patrick McArdle, to enjoy the destruction first-hand. "The first unit treated us like a second unit for one day," Nicholson recalled, "and Joe gave us a real brief storyboard of what he wanted us to do. Then he just let us go to it. Dennis Peterson, an art director and a couple of grips were there, and we just tore the place up. We had a great time." Eager to make the sequence more lively, Dante asked Nicholson to record the action with the plate camera moving, an approach not usually taken when filming background plates. "Generally when we do plate photography, the camera is locked off; and we don't normally do pans or dolly shots or any kind of movement. On Explorers, however, the camera was moving in probably eighty percent of our plates. In Wolf's basement, for instance, Joe wanted us to keep tracking the bubble by moving the plate camera. Such movement did impose certain difficulties when we had to put in a miniature element, a matte painting or the bubble itself. But, overall, it worked out very nicely." Since a lot of the shots in the basement would involve the placement of bubble effects in the plates, Nicholson decided to first shoot a reference plate before the final plates were filmed. "We had storyboards for the sequence, but they were really not that accurate in terms of what we ended up doing. So we ultimately shot a reference pass with Joe in which he actually took a white croquet ball and moved around the set to show us where he wanted the bubble to go. Of course, we knew the ball would go much faster in the final version, but this pass gave us reference points for plotting the movement of our bubble. We used those points in plotting out the moves on our animation stand. That way, the animators could rotoscope the reference plate, find those plot points in the actual plate, and then plan the move of the forcefield based on those reference points." While the reference plates proved very helpful and were considered almost moving storyboards, they did not always predict the movement of the forcefield. The speed of the sphere was roughly determined during postproduction and, in certain shots, it had to do loops and other moves in order to kill time between two different physical effects. "For some shots," Nicholson explained, "we couldn't have it go straight from point A to point B because then it would be going too slow. For example, if the bubble was supposed to hit a steampipe and then go through the refrigerator, and the cut was maybe 100 frames long, the ball might have to do some extra calisthenics to keep the speed consistent." The next time the bubble makes an appearance in the film occurs when the boys begin experimenting with it out on a hilltop. During this attempt to understand how better to control the force, they realize that it can be made larger and larger - and soon Wolfgang finds himself accidentally trapped inside the field. In this scene, the sphere is a larger version of the one that appeared earlier, and the same optical techniques were used to create it - although the shots were overall more complicated because they involved the boy. To place him within the field, actor River Phoenix was bluescreened at ILM using a special rig that was also employed in the flying dream sequence at the end of the film. "It was actually a body mold with a side mount on it," Nicholson explained, "and he was sort of in a tucked-up position. With the rig, we could spin him in circles, turn him upside down and have him move from side to side - we got him dizzy a few times. Then there was camera movement on top of that, which Don Dow shot using a Chapman 'Olympian' crane. For that sequence, the animation of the bubble was photographed as a match move to the bluescreen element of the boy." During the bluescreen work, Phoenix was filmed primarily at 24 frames per second; but occasionally 32 frames were used to smooth out his action and to help create the sensation that he was floating inside the bubble. To further enhance the entrapment effect, the background behind him in the bubble was distorted as it had been in the basement scene. "We had to make sure that it was a little bit cloudy the day we shot the background plate," Rodis recalled, "because we could only show the distortion if there was a texture there to distort. If it was just against a blue sky there would have been nothing to distort." At first, Wolf's accidental entrapment seems to be harmless enough, but then all hell breaks loose when the field becomes uncontrollable. It flies up into the air and then back towards the ground and then up again until it finally goes crashing into the hillside and begins digging a tunnel that could take it on an unexpected journey to the center of the earth. "The first shot of when he actually makes impact was done as a plate filmed in Petaluma," Nicholson explained. "There was a rigged hole in the ground set with a charge by ILM's Ted Moehnke and crew. When the shot begins, the camera is looking at the spot where the hole will be from ten feet away. Then, when the charge is exploded, the camera moves in and up over the hole, looking down into it after Wolf has supposedly entered and plowed into the earth. For the actual element of Wolf in the bubble, we shot a motion control puppet of Wolf and then added the animated element of the bubble. Once he gets inside and he's sort of burrowing down into the earth, we added one shot where you actually look back up at the tunnel that he's burrowed through. That was done using a miniature which we built at ILM, a bluescreen element of Wolf, and then some animated dirt elements that we shot to drop down into the tunnel." Soon after this groundbreaking experience, Wolf emerges from the earth and Ben manages to shut off the field. Because there is a limited amount of air inside the field, Wolf is a little dazed but unharmed, inspiring Ben to take a little test spin of his own. Soon, the boys realize that if the forcefield can hold one person, it can hold three; and if it can hold three, then it can hold a spaceship. As a result of this discovery, the youthful adventurers make a late-night raid on a nearby junkyard and find the necessary parts to construct their own makeshift vessel which they promptly christen the Thunder Road. From this unusual vantage point, the boys watch with nervous amusement as some dogs in a neighbor's yard start barking at the hovering ship. In reality, the section above the fence was a matte painting of the neighborhood, and the dogs were actually trained animals that had been filmed as foreground action while their trainer stood on the fence enticing them to bark. The boys soon leave their neighborhood behind and fly towards a drive-in movie theater where a cheap science fiction thriller called Starkilleris playing on the screen - a movie that, like most 'B' films, has a rather peculiar history. "We originally were going to use some scenes from a 1960 Japanese movie called Battle in Outer Space, "Dante recalled, "but Toho Studios wanted more money for the use of the scenes than I think they spent to make the entire movie. It did have a semi-cheesy quality which seemed to be appropriate for what we wanted, but Originally, Dante had planned to shoot his own interior scenes and use clips from the Japanese film just for the exterior shots. To make this final dream a successful one visually, the team at ILM had to conquer the problem that has plagued every film involving a human in flight - making it look convincing. "There are a lot of different ways of doing flying effects," Dante added, "but ILM came up with a new one which allows the foreground and the background to have more connection with one another without the random size changes and other things that always seemed off in previous pictures. And their approach worked flawlessly. There were things we wanted to do that the system couldn't, but the things that we really needed to do worked fine - and I think were inherently less dangerous. For instance, I understand that for Supergirl, Helen Slater was flown around on a guy wire a hundred feet up off the ground. Well, you can't do that with little kids. They just might have some reservations of their own as to whether or not they want to do a thing like that The approach ILM developed involved filming the foreground footage of the actors first, and then shooting miniature clouds with camera moves that matched those made earlier while photographing the kids. "When we first approached the sequence," said Dow, "we thought about using wires and the standard techniques that have been used in the past for flying people around. We also thought about doing it motion control with puppets. Ultimately, however, we decided to marry the two together and do motion control but use live people instead of puppets. So we had our stage crew build some pretty elaborate model-movers or tracking systems similar to those we use to film miniatures, and adapted them to support the kids. We did this by first building a pylon with a large eight-foot square bluescreen behind it. The pylon was horizontal - coming out the center of the screen - and was designed to rotate and have roll and yaw capability. Then we had to have some way of mounting the kids onto the pylon, so we built some very thin fiberglass suits that contoured to their bodies and were strong enough to support their weight." The fiberglass body suits, hidden beneath the actors' clothing, were connected to the central pole by a rod that came out the side. For each actor, three different rigs were actually built - one with the connecting bar on the right side of the actor, one on the left, and one behind for shots showing the kids flying directly at the camera. The various rods were then masked in bluescreen material. In addition to the movement created in the rigs themselves, the camera was mounted to allow further flexibility. "For the broad movements of flying back and forth," Dow explained, "the camera had to do the moving, not the kids on the mounts. So, we decided that we had to use some kind of system to mount the camera - our highspeed VistaVision 'Empireflex' - and eventually settled on the Chapman 'Olympian' crane. It had the capability of going about eighteen miles per hour at maximum speed, and that was what we needed in order to move the camera back and forth fairly rapidly, Basically, what we were really doing was motion control, but shooting it at normal speed - 24 frames per second. We had people operating the roll, the rack and the yaw positioning of the kids; and at the same time, we had people running the camera crane back and forth as well as moving a boom. As the camera operator, I performed the camera tilt and pan functions. Of course, with puppets you can repeat your moves over and over; but with kids we couldn't do that, so we had to do several takes until we got the best moves. The key to the filming was getting everybody coordinated. We did that by plotting our moves out ahead of time and making marks for the chassis to go through. We would then have somebody call out those marks, and each person would have to be at their designated point. That's how we were able to repeat the moves fairly well. They were not repeatable to the extent that we could put one element over the other or anything like that. However, they were close enough that if we had two or three kids in a shot, we could choreograph each successive move so that they would be at a certain point at a certain time. "It was a very complicated system," affirmed Dante, "and when we walked in there was this long ramp, and on the ground were thousands of numbers with little crosses on them. These were position points for where the actors' rigs and the camera had to be at any given time in the sequence. It was all far beyond me. They really were entirely on their own as far as the camera work was concerned. I just told the kids when to look up, when to say what they had to say and what they were supposed to be thinking and seeing." Once the live-action bluescreen work with the young actors was finished, Dow proceeded to film the miniature clouds that would serve as backgrounds for the flying sequence. "The reason it was decided I should do the clouds was the fact that I had previously filmed the kids, and the movement on the kids really dictated the move that we put on the miniature clouds. We knew the trickiest part of the sequence was making sure that the moves would match as closely as possible; and since I knew what I had been thinking when I choreographed the camera moves on the kids, I could easily transfer those thoughts to the clouds." Before Dow could begin, however, Dante carefully went through all of the takes of the kids and chose the ones he thought were best. "It was pretty hard for him to select those without seeing the clouds," Dow explained, "but we had to have him choose what action he liked best. The fact that we were able to repeat our moves pretty closely meant that whatever action he liked on the kids we could match to the clouds, with some minor variations." The billowy, fluffy clouds that appear in the sequence were actually made of polyester fiberfill material that was filmed against black at half-second exposures using the Dykstraflex motion control camera. "In the opening shot, we look up at a layer of clouds, move up and go through them. For this shot, we mounted the clouds on netting - a bridal veil-type of material. Then, for the rest of the sequence, which is actually above this

main cloud layer, model clouds were placed on black velvet to give them that flat bottom look like they are part of an inversion layer - like a sea of clouds, with an occasional break in the sea to reveal the computer landscape below. We also had some clouds suspended up above this main layer, which were attached to pieces of plastic or netting held up by C-stands covered with black velvet. The additional floating clouds gave some dimension to the set." Originally, the cloud set measured approximately sixteen feet square, but it was eventually expanded to sixteen by forty feet, thus providing enough clouds to track over at the desired speed of movement. The look of the cloud set was enhanced by fog filters placed on the camera to create a greater sense of atmosphere. "We were trying to get away from the dry ice look of things," Dow noted. "Also, our clouds were mostly cumulouslooking; and we didn't want movement in them as such because we found that when you go up in an airplane, real clouds don't appear to move that much - they look pretty stationary." While dry ice was not used in any of the shots of the clouds, a liquid nitrogen element was photographed for the dissolve at the beginning of the sequence when the camera moves up through the cloud layer. In that shot, the frame goes white for a split second and then the point of view appears to be coming up out of the cloud bank. (Originally, the first two dream sequences were to contain only POV shots. But when preview audiences expressed confusion, some last-minute scene-shuffling was effected. Hence, the cloud passage - designed for incorporation into the final dream - eventually ended up in the first, preceding a similarly uprooted shot of Ben flying through the skies.) Besides making good use of foreground and background shots in the sequence, ILM's efforts to create a believable-looking flight were aided by a decision made early on - the sequence would be set against a dark blue night sky. A bright light source like the sun would have required that the source be matched perfectly in each shot. "We thought by having a moonlit night we could use a soft key light that we could easily maintain continuity with," Dow explained. "We also felt that with a weak key light, we would be able to get by if it didn't always match just perfectly in every shot." For all concerned, creating the effects for Explorers proved to be a race against time. "On Gremlins, we had a year of preproduction during which we made another picture, and a year of postproduction," Dante recalled. "On Explorers, however, we had about three months. We all ended up working seven days a week trying to get the picture to be as good as it could be in the time that we had. Everybody was knocking themselves out - people like Ralph Winter and everyone at ILM, Omnibus and Rob Bottin's shop - making it incumbent on me to try and find a way to make the picture turn out to be pretty good." The end result, Dante hopes, is a nice tale about believing enough in your dreams to make them come true. "Then again, it could mean that if you really believe in your dreams, you can get your movie out by July 12th." Standard rotoscoping is the technique of projecting an image onto a sheet of paper for the purpose of tracing selected outlines. Photo-roto differs from traditional rotoscoping in only one major procedure - instead of placing normal punched animation paper on the stand to trace a projected positive point, a similarly-sized sheet of punched photographic paper is used. Using the roto setup as an enlarger, each frame of a black-andwhite duplicate negative is photographed and developed, generating punched photographic prints which can be overlayed with clear animation cels and traced to the heart's content of the animator. The generated art is then photographed by converting the projector back into a camera and shooting the art in the exact same 1:1 ratio. Not only does photo-roto offer the opportunity to produce superior matte work and intricate interactive animation, it also frees the roto camera for more pressing jobs by eliminating the quandary of conventional rotoscoping - the inability to shoot and rotoscope at the same time. Problem was, they'd already shot the action involving one of the characters being picked up by the thing with a three-clawed hand and larger arm than the real tyrannosaurus. Even with the longer arms, it didn't seem realistic that he could lean over and pick someone up. Also, they wanted a 'blocky' kind of head. An actual T-Rex with close-set eyes probably doesn't look as menacing as the fantasy of how it should look. In movies - especially Disney movies - it's always been presented as huge and menacing. I would have preferred to have done it more realistically." Reservations aside, Hester attempted to keep the customers satisfied while „aintaining the painstaking realism for which Rick Baker and he are renowned. Hester obtained a detailed tyrannosaurus skeleton schematic from vertebrate paleontologist Mary Odano which served as a reference point. Working with Rae's armature, Hester first constructed a ribcage-shaped housing from wire with orthopedic casting bandages for the breathing mechanism. That accomplished, Hester sculpted the beast directly onto the armature in standard Roma 3 clay. Although Hester at Baker's EFX and the mechanics contingent at Beswick's facility stayed in constant contact, the sculpture needed frequent fine-tuning. At Betuel's and Scheele's request, hester rendered the beast's arms "less human in musculature" as well as resculpting the head in the "craggy old muscle-builder" image for which the filmmakers opted. With Hester being otherwise granted wide artistic berth, however, the sculpture departed even further from the Scheele original. "The first beast was younger-looking, but I went for broke with extremely deep wrinkles," Hester said. "Looking at other animals and photographs, I made a comparison as to where things wrinkle and muscles tend to bulge. Since the torso and legs were cast separately, sculpting deeper wrinkles around the thighs and backs of the legs allowed me to hide the foam join better. Wrinkles allow skin folds to compress, so I used a loop sculpting tool to break it up and keep it from looking too regular. Then I added cross-wrinkles across those. For example, when the head turned, I wanted the wrinkles to collapse in that spot. If it had been smooth, it would have tended to buckle in the wrong spot. On the full-sized beast, I guess they didn't have too much time, so they didn't really mind that I went off-track." Hester completed his sculpture in approximately three weeks, roughing in certain aspects - such as the inner mouth, forearms and claws - for later refinement once the creature had evolved. "Once the sculpture was finished," Hester said, "I took a wire and slowly cut off the tail and legs, being very careful to do it within the deep wrinkles. The armature was such that I could experiment and do things like take off the arms all through the sculpting process." Since the puppet would be filmed at high-speed, Hester and company envisioned it performing rapid actions and therefore wanted to include such perfectionistic elements as a pendulous throat. Those plans, however, were scrapped. Hester took a brief respite from the project while Tim Lawrence and Shawn McEnroe joined forces to make the molds. The moldmakers used Ultracal 30 with sisal reinforcement, despite their reservations about the industry-standard ored gypsum cement. "Years ago, you could bake Ultracal without it wearing out or breaking," said McEnroe. "Now the stuff goes so quickly, people have to resort to making multiple molds or going to silicones or fiberglass. Like many materials we use in this business, the quality's just not there any more." In two weeks' time, Lawrence and McEnroe generated twentyseven separate mold pieces with cores. The head and body section was comprised of seven pieces with a two-piece core, the arms two pieces each, the legs four, and the tail two pieces with a base plug. "We had to be very careful where we located the seam lines so they'd be easy to deal with in the final piece," commented Lawrence, who took on molding and plastic partmaking jobs as a trade-off for performing some puppeteer functions. "We used machined aluminum parts in the body cores to represent some of the mechanics - for instance, the

length between the head and body - so the mechanics would have an exact nesting place when the foam pieces were fitted over the finished mechanical armature." Although their tasks proved fairly straightforward, both men noted aspects which might have gone more smoothly. "In making the fiberglass parts for the hollow head and body pieces," Lawrence said, "we had to make some separate molds off the cores just so we could lay fiberglass into it. In retrospect, we decided we could have gotten away with making fiberglass molds, which could have been made lighter and with a lot fewer pieces. But we all agreed with Doug. With such a tight schedule, he didn't feel confident trying something new at the time." With the molds completed, Tony Gardner - a member of Baker's contingent for the past two years - came on to run the foam pieces. The foam was industry-standard Schram foam, now produced by the Burman Studios. "The mold was in sections and it took two people to pick it up," said Gardner, who was more accustomed to the kind of smaller cosmetic pieces he had produced for the Thriller video, Into the Night and Return of the Living Dead. "We didn't have the facilities to do the mold in one giant batch of foam, so we had to run two separate batches. A normal-size batch is 150 grams - these were 1050. It took two of those to fill the body, plus 500 grams extra for the arms and legs." The creature's hands, feet and legs having been cast with the mechanics already in place necessitated Gardner's sealing over the joints with balloons and condoms to prevent foam from seeping into the mechanics. "We went through the first pair of arms that way. It's nerve-wracking to run batches this large and get a high volume at the same time. A regular volume on foam is basically four to seven times the volume one starts out with. We were trying to push that to eight or nine so we would have something that wouldn't strain the dinosaur's mechanics. Without using any additives and by simply experimenting with room temperature, mixing ratios and mixing times, we were able to get a consistent high volume with good cell structure and skin around eleven to thirteen volumes. Of course, when we tried to pour the foam into an injector, it was like meringue. And care had to be taken not to introduce air into it, which would have broken down the cell structure and caused air bubbles that would have left pit marks on the surface." Gardner's experimentation resulted in foam with high volume, more stable cell structure, and improved consistency and durability - all elements considered impossible at that level under ordinary conditions. With the foam pieces completed, Tom Hester returned and, aided by Shawn McEnroe -who devised the creature's color scheme and did all the final painting -added the finishing touches involving the mechanics, fitting the foam over the armature and cosmetics. Considering how much independent construction had gone on, it was not surprising that minor adjustments were necessitated. "Certain things like the shoulders and shoulder sockets weren't exactly in line," admitted Hester. "The hips were also a little bit wide: but it was almost 66 • CINEFEX 23

The misfits meant that Hester and McEnroe needed to build, insert and repaint small foam pieces for matching purposes. Other revisions were aesthetic. "I wanted a range of movement under the arms," continued Hester. "When the creature lifted its arms, I wanted the flesh of the armpits to stretch out; when the arms were down, I wanted it to compress." To compensate for the arms having been sculpted in the anatomically correct 'down' position, Hester and McEnroe layered in carefully-cut pieces from another skin, bonding them with Kraton contact cement. For the inner mouth design, Hester vetoed the customary quick-fix fabric construct, since Betuel and Scheele planned on giving the head and mouth a fair amount of on-camera scrutiny. "That was another production," Hester laughed. "As a lizard opens its mouth, you can see these sort of flaps on the side, so I wanted to have a translucent material. However, it had to stretch as the mouth opened and couldn't buckle when the mouth closed." When his initial solution of Hot-Melt vinyl didn't withstand the stress of repeated takes, Hester replaced it with balloon rubber. "They were just very simple flaps glued to the skull with the skin overlapping - and they had to be changed every so often because the mouth got a lot of abuse constantly opening and closing." To simulate the tyrannosaurus' saber-like teeth, Hester sculpted directly onto a fiberglass skull from one of the core molds, building the bridge of the mouth, then approximating the eventual position of the jaw hinge with Doug Beswick, who built a temporary guidepost hinge. Rather than actually sculpting fifty tiny teeth separately, Hester opted for carving with dental wax. The wax not only proved able to withstand repeated removal and repositioning of the teeth, but also the frequent opening and closing of the mouth for checking bite alignment. To avoid adding extra weight and stress to the neck - under which the mechanics were cantilevered - Hester made the creature's gums a virtual shell. The Hester-devised teeth and mouth pieces were then installed in the Notaro-built jaw mechanics. Notaro cut a fiberglass section from the skull, then placed two pivot points at the creature's actual pivot points, which were discerned from the full-sized skull on hand at the shop. For tongue movement, Hester adapted a solution he'd arrived at while devising Starman's starchild. "The tongue presented some of the same difficulties as the baby's hand. In such a tiny hand, there was no way of getting actual metal mechanics in there. I did a prototype tongue in Hot-Melt but, aside from durability problems, there was a weight problem again. I took a polyethylene tube, cut wedges out of it so it would arch up while the tip of the tongue came up the other way in an S-curve. I ran a cable through it. By pulling a thread, it would collapse. So wherever there were wedges, it would bend." While the effects work was underway, producer Taplin and effects supervisor Scheele requested Beswick and crew to bump up their completion date by two weeks. Beswick accommodated the request, necessitating Shawn McEnroe's painting and detailing the beast on a nonstop work jag. "We got the finished tail mechanics for the dinosaur on Saturday," McEnroe explained, "and had to put it together, apply the skin, patch it, paint it and deliver it by Monday. It should have taken three-and-a-half days to do. We had a day and a half. " As a color guide for McEnroe's chores, he and John Scheele tore off a chunk of the full-scale tyrannosaurus lying in state on the Disney backlot. It proved of only moderate help, however, since California sun and smog had already altered it considerably. In addition to the full-function puppet, a nonarticulated 'stand-in' was also produced. "The stand-in was a foam replica on a polyfoam core," explained McEnroe, "just to take light readings off. I'd painted it a fairly bright green because I was working with colors on that skin patch. I showed it to John Scheele and he suggested taking it down to make it look a lot more brown." On the second pass, McEnroe and Hester shifted the color away from the lizardy greens to more weathered, mottled ochres and browns. The paints were standard-issue and mixed with rubber cement and benzene solvent - as much reputed for its facility in creating 'layered color' effects as for its poisonous and carcinogenic qualities. "For a number of reasons," said McEnroe, "I wished we'd gone to something like Dick Smith's paints, which are half acrylic and half Pros-aide, a prosthetic adhesive - but this worked out better because the rubber cement impregnates the latex surface and the dinosaur took a lot of wear during filming. Another advantage with rubber cement benzene was that because Tony had to run six or seven skins, each new skin lost more and more of the incredible detail Tom had sculpted in. If you're crafty, you can paint some of that texture back on." Beswick delivered the mechanical dinosaur a week earlier than originally specified. "The producers thought it would be to their benefit if we finished earlier since they'd have that much more lead time on the opticals and so forth," Beswick recalled. But the dead-heat scheduling had its downside. Beswick delivered the beast on March 14, test shots were done the following day and actual production commenced on March 18. "Ted Rae and I got together a week before and did some test walks so that the film crew could determine the appropriate speeds. Aside from that, everything else was done on-set. Trying to work with conventional lighting instruments was introducing a softer, 'mushier' look to the scenes. "Norm had been advising from the sidelines," Scheele continued, "but was now able to come in with King Baggot and develop a lighting solution - under real pressure-cooker conditions. Norm felt it best to forget the speed flexibility and re-establish the look of the HMIs which have inherently a sharper, more chiseled effect. So basically we called a halt over the weekend after seeing the difference on film. The new shots just brought the detail to life, especially in closeups." Huddling in the editorial trailer, the decision was made to reshoot about half the sequence, most notably the opening cuts. The effects crew was naturally upset that so much of their recent effort appeared to have been in vain. Not the least of their concerns was the fact that the tyrannosaurus had already been put through considerable abuse. BB gun fire and air mortars used to simulate gunfire had damaged the skin surface; and dinosaur 'blood' had soaked into the foam and hardened up, affecting flexibility, particularly in the neck. "By the end of the first week," Tom Hester commented, "the dinosaur was basically hamburger." He and Shawn McEnroe put in some long hours restoring the animal to near-new condition. Since there had never been any serious rehearsal time with the whole crew, Scheele reasoned that this storm cloud was not without its silver lining. "Rick's approach to bringing a creature on-line often means serious rehearsal only just before the camera is ready to roll. All the individual mechanics had been tested out, and we'd done some film and video tests. But it all kind of came together on the set. Only then could the operators really put it together. For instance, we never could absolutely know how the walk was going to work out. It was never perfect - but since it was seen for no more than half a step in any one cut, it never really had to be. Likewise, the collapse of the rex was an awkward piece of business for a rod puppet, and Doug couldn't demonstrate it in advance - it all had to happen on the set. So now we had the luxury of considering much of that first week as very expensive rehearsal time. Fortunately, since we had come in so far under budget in the live-action phase of production, we were able to go to the powers that be and ask to continue shooting." The last dinosaur shot to go to camera was a brief, full-frame insert of the beast's stomach exploding under the impact of a grenade. To achieve the shot, Shawn McEnroe stayed on to prepare and dress a stand-in tyrannosaurus. McEnroe began by cutting a large hole in the puppet s stomach area and making an alginate mold from that, with a duplicate positive mold in Ultracal. "I tried using a gelatin appliance for the stomach at first," said McEnroe, "but since they were using air pressure to blow it out, no amount of glue could withstand that. I had to go to a precut polyfoam appliance, which I cut into six pieces and carefully reassembled. Then I just patched it with K-Y jelly and face powder to match the stomach color. The blood was Karo syrup and food coloring and I cut out rolled-foam hearts, livers and entrails, hoping the camera would pick them up but knowing it wouldn't." Joe-type' doll pants and shoes over his fingers and waggled appropriately. Compositing and final enhancement of the sequence began even as Beswick and crew were signing off. Photo-rotos of the dinosaur backgrounds were initiated for scenes involving gunfire or interactive light, with the gunflash elements themselves generated as airbrush artwork by Bill Arance. Gary Trousdale even penciled in some pterodactyls flying through the opening cuts. "We had the pleasure of pulling the original Fantasia artwork and referring to it for this element," Scheele recalled. "Even though the cels from that period were trashed because of the fire hazard, one of the advantages of working at Disney is that you can access this priceless material, check it out for study, and not need to reinvent the wheel, so to speak." Even though it was an exhausting shoot, everyone was satisfied with the final effort. "It's a pretty ambitious undertaking on everybody's part to try and have a full rod puppet really walk around," commented Beswick. "I think it's something everybody's going to be really impressed with. It does have a different look than stop-motion." Scheele hedged his bet just slightly: "I was about eighty percent satisfied as we wrapped - which I think is probably high. It was our first dive into this kind of miniature, and there were plenty of complications along the way, It was a real challenge, though, and a terrific team effort. On the screen, I think the action is such that the imperfections can be perceived by the trained eye, but not felt in the flow of the action. We can all get a little caught up in the auteur aspects of creature control; but in the final analysis, this movie is more a Ghostbusters than a My Dinner with Andre.
